opening: Our social network's feed is ranked by a few hand-tuned rules and people say it's stale. Design a machine learning system that ranks the news feed.

clarifications.answer: About 2 billion daily users, opening the feed around 8 times a day.
A typical person has about 1,500 eligible posts since their last visit from friends, followed pages and groups.
The first screen must render within 300 ms; more posts load as they scroll.
The goal is meaningful interactions between people and daily return visits, not time spent at any cost.
Spam, clickbait and misinformation must be demoted or removed; integrity rules change often.
Some posts come from accounts the person doesn't follow; they should appear only when clearly valuable.
We log impressions, dwell time, likes, comments, shares, hides, reports and occasional 'is this worth your time' survey answers.

clarificationPolicy: Answer as the feed product lead. Keep it a very large, multi-objective ranking problem with integrity constraints; decide unlisted details so the value model, integrity and freshness stay central.

agenda.goal: Establish scale, candidates per request, latency and the real objective.
agenda.opener: What would you like to understand about the feed and its goals before designing?

evidence.strong: Asks about users and loads per day, eligible posts per viewer, latency, the objective, integrity rules and available feedback signals; recognises engagement alone can reward harmful content.
evidence.adequate: Gets scale and latency but takes engagement as the only goal.
evidence.weak: Designs without asking about scale or goals.

misconceptions.pattern: Assumes maximising time spent is the goal.
misconceptions.challenge: Outrage keeps people scrolling. Is that the feed the company wants?

probes: What does a good feed mean for the person and for the company?
How many posts compete for the first screen?
hints: The size of the candidate set shapes the architecture.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Billions of feed loads, around 1,500 candidates each, a tight first-screen budget, and an objective of meaningful interactions with integrity constraints.

agenda.goal: Define how predictions become one ranking score.
agenda.opener: What exactly would the model predict, and how would you turn that into a ranking?

evidence.strong: Predicts probabilities of several actions (like, comment, share, long dwell, hide, report) and ranks by a weighted value function with negative weights for hides and reports; weights are tuned by experiments on long-term outcomes; heads are calibrated.
evidence.adequate: Predicts engagement but combines signals vaguely.
evidence.weak: Ranks by predicted clicks or recency only.

misconceptions.pattern: Treats all actions as equally valuable.
misconceptions.challenge: Is a like worth the same as a thoughtful comment from a close friend?

probes: How are the weights between actions chosen?
Why must the predicted probabilities be calibrated?
hints: Several predictions can feed one formula.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Calibrated predictions for several positive and negative actions combined in a weighted value function tuned by experiments.

agenda.goal: Lay out the ranking pipeline within the latency budget.
agenda.opener: Walk me through what happens when someone opens the feed.

evidence.strong: Gathers inventory from friends, pages and groups plus recommended posts, applies integrity filters, a light ranker trims to hundreds, a heavy multi-task ranker scores them, a final pass enforces diversity and freshness; ranks more than one page and returns the first, with per-stage budgets.
evidence.adequate: Retrieval and ranking but no integrity step or budgets.
evidence.weak: Sorts all posts with one model per request.

misconceptions.pattern: Uses one heavy model on all eligible posts.
misconceptions.challenge: Thousands of posts times hundreds of thousands of loads a second: what's the bill?

probes: What do you do when they scroll to the next page?
hints: Filter and narrow before the expensive model.
Later pages can use fresher signals.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Inventory plus recommended candidates, integrity filtering, a light then heavy ranker, a final diversity and freshness pass, ranking ahead of scrolling.

agenda.goal: Choose and serve the features that matter most for feed ranking.
agenda.opener: Which features would carry the most signal, and how fresh do they need to be?

evidence.strong: Viewer-author affinity from past interactions, post type and age, early engagement velocity from a stream, viewer's history with similar posts, friends' engagement on the post, context; served from a feature store with stream-updated counters.
evidence.adequate: Lists reasonable features but not freshness or how they're computed.

misconceptions.pattern: Thinks global popularity is the strongest signal.
misconceptions.challenge: A viral post from a stranger versus a close friend's update: which does the person care about?

probes: How would you compute how close two people are?
How quickly must engagement counts update?
hints: Relationships matter in a social feed.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Affinity, post type and age, stream-updated engagement velocity, viewer history and friends' engagement served from a feature store.

agenda.goal: Keep harmful and low-quality posts down without retraining the ranker for every policy change.
agenda.opener: How do spam, clickbait and misinformation stay out of the top of the feed?

evidence.strong: Separate integrity classifiers per issue, applied as hard filters for violations and multiplicative demotions for borderline content, so policy changes don't require retraining the engagement model; outrage-bait counteracted with quality signals and surveys.
evidence.adequate: Adds a filter for bad content but folds everything into the ranker.
evidence.weak: Assumes engagement ranking will handle it.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes the engagement model will learn to avoid harmful posts.
misconceptions.challenge: If misleading posts get more comments, what does an engagement model learn?

probes: Why keep integrity models separate from the ranker?
What's the difference between removing and demoting?
hints: Policy changes faster than ranking models retrain.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Separate per-issue integrity classifiers applied as filters or demotions, independent of the engagement ranker.

agenda.goal: Keep the feed fresh and varied across repeated visits.
agenda.opener: Someone opens the feed, closes it, and opens it again ten minutes later. What do they see?

evidence.strong: Tracks seen posts and demotes them unless there's new activity, caches the ranked list briefly for navigation, re-ranks on new sessions with fresh signals, pre-ranks when a session is likely, and applies author and type diversity rules.
evidence.adequate: Removes seen posts but no caching or diversity plan.

misconceptions.pattern: Recomputes the full ranking on every scroll event.
misconceptions.challenge: What does that cost, and do people notice the difference between scrolls?

probes: How do you avoid ten posts from one page in a row?
When would you rank ahead of time?
hints: Rules in a final pass control repetition.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Seen-post tracking, brief caching, fresh re-ranking per session, opportunistic pre-ranking and diversity rules.

agenda.goal: Prove changes help in the long run.
agenda.opener: How would you know a new ranking change is good for people over months, not days?

evidence.strong: A/B tests on meaningful interactions and return visits with guardrails (hide and report rates, integrity prevalence, survey satisfaction), long-running holdouts to catch long-term harm, and care with novelty effects.
evidence.adequate: An A/B test on engagement with no long-term view.

misconceptions.challenge: A change lifts comments for a week and then retention falls slowly. How would you have seen it?

probes: Which metric would stop a launch even if engagement rose?
Why keep a group on the old system for months?
hints: Short-term and long-term effects can disagree.
agenda.moveOnSummary: A/B tests with integrity and satisfaction guardrails plus long-running holdouts to catch slow harm.

agenda.goal: Meet the latency budget at peak load and degrade gracefully.
agenda.opener: How does ranking stay within the time budget at peak traffic?

evidence.strong: Estimates predictions per second, batches the heavy ranker on GPUs, distils a light ranker, budgets each stage, and falls back to the light ranker's order or a cached ranking when the heavy model is slow.
evidence.adequate: Mentions caching or scaling but no estimates or fallback.
evidence.weak: Assumes it will be fast enough.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes adding servers alone fixes latency.
misconceptions.challenge: If one request's model call is slow, do more servers make that request faster?

probes: Roughly how many scores per second at peak?
What does the user see when the heavy model times out?
agenda.moveOnSummary: Per-second prediction estimates, GPU batching, a distilled light ranker, per-stage budgets and a fallback ranking.

agenda.goal: Summarise the main trade-offs and risks.
agenda.opener: What trade-offs did you make, and what worries you most about this design?

evidence.strong: Discusses engagement versus wellbeing, friends versus recommended content, freshness versus cost, weight tuning, and monitoring of integrity and satisfaction.

probes: How do you balance friends' posts with recommendations?
What metric would you never let drop?
hints: Think about what the company could lose by optimising the wrong thing.
Blending policies are product decisions too.
agenda.moveOnSummary: Engagement versus wellbeing, friends versus recommendations, and freshness versus cost, watched through integrity and satisfaction metrics.

curveballs.prompt: Your new model lifted comments by a lot, but a review finds the extra comments are mostly angry arguments under misleading posts. What do you change?
People who open the app several times an hour complain they keep seeing the same posts. Where does your design fall short?

alternatives.choice: Separate models per action instead of one multi-task model
alternatives.whenBetter: When teams own different objectives or tasks conflict strongly; simpler to debug, more to serve.

alternatives.choice: Gradient-boosted trees as the heavy ranker
alternatives.whenBetter: With mostly dense engineered features and a smaller team; less suited to sparse ids and embeddings.

alternatives.choice: Chronological feed with light ML re-ranking
alternatives.whenBetter: For products where recency and user control matter more than engagement, such as messaging-like feeds.

exemplars.label: Value model with integrity
exemplars.outline: Clarifies scale, about 1,500 candidates per load, the latency budget and the meaningful-interactions goal. Defines a value function over calibrated predictions of positive and negative actions with experiment-tuned weights. Builds inventory and recommended candidates, separate integrity filters and demotions, a light and a multi-task heavy ranker with affinity and engagement-velocity features from a feature store, and a final diversity and freshness pass, ranking ahead of scrolling. Sizes GPU inference with fallbacks, and launches through A/B tests with satisfaction and integrity guardrails and long-term holdouts.

exemplars.label: Engagement ranker
exemplars.outline: Builds a two-stage ranker predicting likes and comments with sensible features and an A/B test, but treats integrity as part of the same model, sums uncalibrated predictions and measures only short-term engagement.

exemplars.label: Popularity sort
exemplars.outline: Sorts posts by total likes and recency with a single model refreshed nightly; no value model, integrity, freshness or evaluation plan.
